findings.condition: authorizeWrite is an OPTIONAL constructor parameter (`authorizeWrite?:(client,stores,global)=>Promise<void>`) and is invoked via optional chaining (`await this.authorizeWrite?.(...)` at line 64 in create() and line 86 in update()). This callback is the ENTIRE enforcement mechanism for Finding B's fix (fresh session/permission/scope re-validation via verifyLedgerWrite immediately before the mutating INSERT/UPDATE, after the inventory/target-row lock wait).
findings.impact: If any current or future call site constructs `new LedgerService(pool, principal)` without the third argument (as every test file in this repo already does, and as a future refactor of ledger-runtime.ts easily could by accident), create()/update() silently skip the post-lock-wait re-authorization and fall back solely to the request-start-time principal snapshot captured by ledgerAccess() in the constructor. This exactly reintroduces the original HIGH-severity Finding B (a permission/session revocation committed while the request was waiting on the 71820600 inventory lock is not honored) with no compile error, lint warning, thrown exception, or test failure signaling the regression — TypeScript accepts the 2-arg call because the parameter is optional, and `?.()` on undefined is a silent no-op rather than a thrown error.
findings.evidence: packages/core/src/catalog/ledger-service.ts:18 (optional parameter declaration); :64 (`await this.authorizeWrite?.(client,...)` in create()); :86 (`await this.authorizeWrite?.(client,...)` in update()). Confirmed by inspection that every non-production call site in this snapshot (scripts/ledger-integration.ts, tests/*) already constructs LedgerService with only 2 arguments, i.e. the 'skip the check' shape is already the common pattern in this codebase, one accidental copy-paste into a production path away from silently disabling B's fix.
findings.fix: Make authorizeWrite a required constructor parameter (drop the `?`), and require every call site (including tests that intentionally bypass it) to pass an explicit stated no-op/test-double, e.g. `async()=>{}`, so omitting real authorization is a deliberate, greppable, type-visible choice rather than the silent default. Alternatively, throw a LedgerError('WRITE_AUTHORITY_NOT_CONFIGURED',500) inside create()/update() when authorizeWrite is undefined, so a missing callback fails closed instead of failing open.
findings.test: Add a unit test that: (1) constructs `new LedgerService(pool, adminPrincipal)` with no third argument, (2) revokes INVENTORY_EDIT for that principal's underlying staff row directly in the DB after construction (simulating a mid-flight revocation), (3) calls `.create()`/`.update()` and asserts the call currently SUCCEEDS despite the revocation (proving the fail-open path), then asserts the fix causes it to throw/fail closed instead.

Independently traced packages/auth/src/accounts.ts writeAccount(): target row is read with `SELECT revision ... FOR UPDATE` and compared against schema-required, bounded `expectedRevision` BEFORE any UPDATE to staff_members/auth_user/access tables; all field mutations (name/active/role/scope/access) commit atomically in one transaction; the committed revision is read fresh from DB (never client-guessed +1) and returned to the caller; acting-admin's own STAFF_MANAGE/scope is independently re-checked (`loadStaff`+`canManage`) after acquiring the sorted advisory locks, so a concurrently-revoked actor cannot complete the write; login/failed-login/password-changed timestamp updates do not touch active/role/scope and correctly do not bump revision (confirmed via migration 0008's staff_guard_audit WHEN-clause and staff_00_settings_boundary WHEN-clause); StaffManagement.tsx correctly surfaces 409/STALE_STAFF_REVISION as a distinct, non-auto-resolving conflict state requiring explicit reload. 23 new S01 tests exercise both admin orderings for disable/role/permission/store-removal plus the acting-admin-revocation race via real Postgres and real UI; my independent trace found this test coverage consistent with the code's actual logic, not merely self-reported.

Independently traced packages/auth/src/ledger-write-authority.ts + packages/core/src/catalog/ledger-service.ts: the ledger transaction acquires the 71820600 inventory/target-row lock(s) FIRST, then (immediately before the mutating INSERT/UPDATE) calls authorizeWrite, which takes a per-subject SHARED advisory lock on namespace 71820901 (held until the ledger transaction's own COMMIT/ROLLBACK) and re-derives permissions fresh via a separate READ ONLY connection to the auth pool (live auth_session row + loadStaff), correctly rejecting on a revoked/expired session or narrowed permissions/scope. accounts.ts's writeAccount() acquires the SAME namespace 71820901 as an EXCLUSIVE lock on sorted [actor, target] keys before any staff_members/access mutation, so PostgreSQL's shared/exclusive contention correctly serializes an in-flight ledger write against a concurrent settings revocation in either arrival order, and a committed revocation is always observed by the ledger write's fresh re-check. Forbidden-store/global-scope checks correctly happen before the inventory lock is even requested (this.checkStore in create(), pre-transaction). Confirmed via 6 new S01 real-Postgres race tests (permission/store/disable revocation during create-wait, target-row-wait, and the reverse-order 'write commits before revocation takes effect' case) that these match the intended protocol. However, see new finding B-FAILOPEN-01: the sole enforcement callback (authorizeWrite) is an OPTIONAL constructor parameter invoked via `?.()`, so a call site that omits it (already the pattern in every test file, and a plausible future refactor mistake in production code) silently reverts to the pre-fix, request-start-only authorization, reintroducing this exact HIGH-severity behavior with no compiler/runtime signal. This does not currently manifest on the one production call site (ledger-runtime.ts correctly wires it), so the fix is assessed RESOLVED for current behavior, with the fail-open design gap tracked as a separate MEDIUM finding rather than reverting this disposition to UNRESOLVED.
